body_text:
The Open Mapping Theorem and Maximum Modulus Principle.

1. **Open Mapping Theorem**: If $U \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ is a
   connected open domain and $f: U \to \mathbb{C}$ is a
   nonconstant holomorphic function, then $f(U)$ is an open subset
   of $\mathbb{C}$. That is, $f$ maps open sets to open sets.

2. **Maximum Modulus Principle**: Let $U \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ be
   a bounded connected domain and let
   $f: \overline{U} \to \mathbb{C}$ be continuous on the closure
   $\overline{U}$ and holomorphic on $U$. Then the modulus
   $|f(z)|$ attains its maximum on the boundary $\partial U$:
   $$ \sup_{z \in U} |f(z)| \le \max_{z \in \partial U} |f(z)|. $$
   Moreover, if $|f(z)|$ attains a local maximum at any interior
   point $z_0 \in U$, then $f$ is identically constant on $U$.

*Proof of Maximum Modulus Principle*: Suppose for contradiction
that $|f|$ attains an interior local maximum at $z_0 \in U$, so
$|f(z)| \le |f(z_0)|$ for all $z$ in some disk
$D(z_0, r) \subseteq U$. If $f$ were nonconstant, the Open Mapping
Theorem implies that the image $f(D(z_0, r))$ is an open
neighborhood of $w_0 = f(z_0)$. But an open disk around $w_0$
necessarily contains points $w$ with $|w| > |w_0|$, contradicting
the assumption that $|f(z_0)|$ was a local maximum. Thus $f$ must
be constant.
